title: A Tree Full of Life
passage:
An old tree can have holes in its trunk and still be alive. Its inner wood may become soft and break down while the living parts continue to grow. Some young insects eat the soft wood. As the wood breaks down, spaces form inside the tree. Birds can build nests in these spaces, and bats can rest there.

So a tree does not have to look perfect to be useful to wildlife. A trunk with holes may hold more life than a visitor first notices. A tree can also provide a home for animals after it dies. Dead wood is part of a living forest, although the tree itself no longer grows. Removing every dead tree would also remove places where some forest animals live.
question: Which statement about old trees agrees with the passage?
correct: Animals can use them before the trees die.
wrong1: Birds can only use them after they die.
wrong2: Their trunks stay hard until the trees die.
wrong3: They stop providing homes after the trees die.
explanation: "An old tree can have holes in its trunk and still be alive." Birds can nest in these spaces, and bats can rest there.
source: Original nonfiction. Facts checked against Forestry England: https://www.forestryengland.uk/blog/protecting-veteran-trees ; https://www.forestryengland.uk/managing-nature
question2: According to the passage, how do birds and insects use these trees differently?
correct2: Birds nest inside them; insects eat soft wood.
wrong1_2: Birds eat soft wood; insects nest inside them.
wrong2_2: Birds use dead trunks; insects need living trees.
wrong3_2: Birds eat their insects; insects eat living leaves.
explanation2: "Some young insects eat the soft wood." Later, "Birds can build nests in these spaces".

title: The Repair Table
passage:
I took my torn bag to the community repair table on Saturday. A neighbour arrived with a radio that had stopped working. The poster said repairs were free, so he expected to take it home working again.

The volunteers checked what each job needed. They had a new zip for my bag, but nobody there was trained to repair electrical equipment. They gave my neighbour the address of a specialist instead. He left with his radio, without paying anything.

I offered to return later for my bag. The volunteer asked me to stay because visitors helped with simple parts of their own repairs. While she replaced the zip, I removed loose threads. There was no charge for the zip either. I left with a working bag and the address of next month's repair session.
question: Why was the radio not repaired at the session?
correct: No volunteer had the training needed for that repair.
wrong1: No volunteer had the replacement part needed for it.
wrong2: Its owner refused to pay the requested repair charge.
wrong3: Its owner left before volunteers could check the problem.
explanation: "nobody there was trained to repair electrical equipment."
source: Original fiction. The session, characters and repair arrangements are invented; no real organisation or research finding is described.
question2: Why did the volunteer ask the narrator to stay?
correct2: Visitors were expected to help with simple repair tasks.
wrong1_2: Visitors were expected to pay before repairs could begin.
wrong2_2: Visitors were expected to provide all necessary replacement parts.
wrong3_2: Visitors were expected to collect repairs at later sessions.
explanation2: "visitors helped with simple parts of their own repairs."

title: Art in the Dark
passage:
A drawing can disappear from a museum wall without being sold or sent for repair. Works on paper are often displayed for limited periods because light can damage both the paper and the materials used to create the image. Even when visitors notice no immediate change, exposure may be causing harm.

Museums therefore control how brightly sensitive works are lit and how long they remain on display. Returning a drawing to storage reduces further exposure; it does not undo damage already caused by light. A carefully repaired tear is a different matter: conservation treatment can address some physical damage without reversing changes caused by light.

Changing the works on display lets visitors encounter different pictures while limiting exposure for individual objects. The collection can remain intact even when the gallery walls look different.
question: Why might a museum replace one displayed drawing with another?
correct: To limit how much light reaches each individual drawing.
wrong1: To reverse damage that light has caused each drawing.
wrong2: To ensure every displayed drawing has first been repaired.
wrong3: To make space exclusively for drawings purchased more recently.
explanation: "Changing the works on display lets visitors encounter different pictures while limiting exposure for individual objects."
question2: Which claim about conservation is supported by the passage?
correct2: Some physical damage can be treated without reversing light damage.
wrong1_2: Light damage becomes reversible once drawings enter suitable storage conditions.
wrong2_2: Protecting paper from light leaves the image materials equally exposed.
wrong3_2: Visible changes must appear before light can harm a drawing.
explanation2: "Returning a drawing to storage reduces further exposure; it does not undo damage already caused by light." Conservation can address "some physical damage".

title: Walking Towards an Idea
passage:
A walk may help when you need ideas, but that does not mean it improves every kind of thinking. In a 2014 study, researchers compared adults' performance on tasks completed while sitting or walking. One task asked for unusual but possible uses for everyday objects. Another required a single word that correctly linked three other words.

Walking helped participants generate creative ideas, but it did not improve performance on the task requiring one correct answer. Some creative benefits also continued briefly after participants sat down again.

Fresh scenery was not necessary for the effect: walking on a treadmill indoors, facing a blank wall, also helped idea generation. These findings support a particular use for walking during creative work. They do not establish that walking improves every stage, from producing possibilities to choosing the best solution.
question: Which task showed a benefit from walking in this study?
correct: Suggesting several unusual but possible uses for everyday objects.
wrong1: Finding the single word that correctly linked other words.
wrong2: Remembering the everyday objects mentioned during an earlier task.
wrong3: Selecting the most practical idea from several suggested uses.
explanation: "Walking helped participants generate creative ideas, but it did not improve performance on the task requiring one correct answer."
source: Original nonfiction describing a real study, without implying universal benefits. Oppezzo and Schwartz (2014), Give Your Ideas Some Legs: https://aaalab.stanford.edu/assets/papers/2014/Give_your_ideas_some_legs.pdf ; Stanford summary: https://ed.stanford.edu/news/study-finds-walking-boosts-creativity
question2: What did the indoor walking results help establish?
correct2: A change of scenery was unnecessary for the creativity benefit.
wrong1_2: Fresh air explained why walking participants produced more original ideas.
wrong2_2: Walking produced its strongest benefits during tasks requiring precise answers.
wrong3_2: Participants needed to continue walking for creative benefits to last.
explanation2: "Fresh scenery was not necessary for the effect: walking on a treadmill indoors, facing a blank wall, also helped idea generation."

title: A Place to Begin
passage:
An arts centre that removes entrance fees may attract more visitors without making it easier for beginners to take part. Watching an exhibition and risking a first attempt at drawing are different experiences. A programme can be publicly available yet still assume that everyone arrives with equipment, confidence and spare time.

I would therefore reserve one evening each week for beginners, with materials provided and no requirement to display finished work. Regular workshops could continue on other evenings. This would extend the programme rather than replace it.

An annual exhibition would still be selected on artistic quality. Places in the beginner sessions, however, would be allocated by application order, not by portfolios. These arrangements serve different purposes: the exhibition presents accomplished work; the sessions give inexperienced people somewhere to start. Attendance figures alone would not tell us whether that second purpose had been achieved.
question: How would places in the proposed beginner sessions be allocated?
correct: By when applications arrive rather than by artistic standard.
wrong1: By artistic standard rather than by when applications arrive.
wrong2: By whether applicants agree to exhibit their finished work.
wrong3: By whether applicants already possess all the necessary equipment.
explanation: "Places in the beginner sessions, however, would be allocated by application order, not by portfolios."
source: Original opinion piece proposing a hypothetical programme. No actual arts centre, attendance data or research results are claimed.
question2: What distinction does the writer make about the proposed programme?
correct2: More visitors would not necessarily mean more beginners were participating.
wrong1_2: Removing entrance fees would eliminate the need for beginner sessions.
wrong2_2: Providing materials would replace artistic quality as the exhibition criterion.
wrong3_2: Regular workshops would stop once the beginner sessions became available.
explanation2: "An arts centre that removes entrance fees may attract more visitors without making it easier for beginners to take part."
